concepts.concept_description: Adding new categories of blocks to the project by selecting an extension. In this case, adding the 'Video Sensing' extension to interact with the webcam.
Using the 'when green flag clicked' block to start the main script of the program, which initializes the video feed.
Using the 'turn video on' block from the Video Sensing extension to activate the user's webcam and display its feed on the Scratch stage.
Using the 'set video transparency to' block to control how visible the webcam feed is. Setting it to 0 makes it fully opaque.
Using the 'forever' block to create a loop that continuously checks for video motion and changes costumes.
Using the 'video motion on sprite' block to get a numerical value representing the amount of movement detected by the camera on the sprite.
Using the '>' operator block to check if the detected video motion value is greater than a specific threshold (e.g., 50).
Using the 'wait until' block to pause the script's execution until a certain condition is true, such as 'video motion > 50'.
Using the 'next costume' block to switch the sprite's appearance to the next one in its costume list, creating the filter-changing effect.
Using the 'wait () seconds' block to pause the program for a specific amount of time between actions, such as keeping a filter on for 3 seconds before changing.
Utilizing the built-in Scratch Paint Editor to draw custom graphics, such as hats, glasses, and mustaches, to be used as costumes for a sprite.
Using the 'when this sprite clicked' event block as an alternative way to trigger an action, specifically to change to the next costume manually.
Understanding the specific order of operations inside a 'forever' loop: wait for motion, change costume, wait for a fixed time. This sequence determines the program's behavior.
Setting up the initial conditions for the project, such as turning the video on and setting its transparency, right after the green flag is clicked.
